news.title: DeepSeek reportedly raises about $15B days after US federal ban
news.summary: DeepSeek has reportedly closed a private round of roughly $15 billion led by Tencent and battery maker CATL. The raise lands just two days after a US order to strip its technology from federal agency systems.

news.title: China clears DeepSeek and MiniMax as its first approved AI exporters
news.summary: According to Chinese state media, DeepSeek and MiniMax are the first companies to finish registration under China's new AI export rules. That clears them to open-source and license their models to users abroad.

news.title: Microsoft says its MAI-DxO system beats doctors on hard diagnostic cases
news.summary: A paper in Science reports that Microsoft's multi-agent diagnosis system solved 83% of complex New England Journal of Medicine case studies. Primary-care doctors working alone got 36% right on the same cases.

news.title: Claude writes formal proofs for 123 open-source libraries and turns up hidden bugs
news.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team and Theorem used Claude to produce machine-checked Rocq proofs for 239 fuzz-test entry points across 123 open-source libraries. The effort surfaced hundreds of bugs that ordinary testing had missed.

news.title: OpenAI's models and Codex are coming to Google Cloud
news.summary: Google Cloud customers will be able to use OpenAI's frontier models and Codex through Model Garden and buy them via Google Cloud Marketplace. Eligible firms can count existing Google Cloud spending commitments toward them, with general availability due in the coming weeks.

news.title: Google DeepMind researchers quit over military AI work
news.summary: Research engineer Sofia Liguori resigned this week and researcher Andreas Kirsch left earlier in October, the BBC reports, amid doubts that Google can see or control how the Pentagon uses its AI. Google says its public-sector contracts go through compliance reviews.

news.title: Big AI labs hand four agent projects to the Linux Foundation
news.summary: The Agentic AI Foundation took in four projects at AGNTCon: Agent Skills, Open Responses, OpenEnv and OpenSandbox. They were contributed by Anthropic, OpenAI, Hugging Face and Alibaba, putting shared agent plumbing under neutral governance.

news.title: Nvidia lines up six suppliers to expand AI hardware capacity
news.summary: Announced around GTC Berlin, the deals expand substrate, interposer, testing and optical-engine capacity through 2028, including a planned 2.5x rise in substrate capacity. Nvidia also showed a prefabricated, container-style Vera Rubin data-center pod meant to cut build times from months to days.

news.title: US Treasury proposes curbs on American investment in Chinese AI
news.summary: A proposed rule implementing the 2025 outbound investment law would restrict US investment in AI and supercomputing in China and other countries of concern. It is now open for public comment.

news.title: China-linked hackers used an agentic AI pentest tool to breach ConnectWise
news.summary: Microsoft ties a supply-chain attack through ConnectWise Cloud Backup to the China-aligned group Storm-0940. The attackers used the ARTEX agentic penetration-testing framework to run password sprays against Microsoft 365 tenants at scale.

news.title: Rivian buys world-model startup Third Dimension for robotaxi simulation
news.summary: Rivian acquired Third Dimension, a 15-person London startup that turns images and video into 3D worlds that can be simulated. It will feed Rivian's self-driving and robotaxi work; terms were not disclosed.

news.title: Micron workers in Taiwan stage the island's first chip-industry strike
news.summary: Micron's Taoyuan union held a one-day strike on October 22, demanding that 15% of operating profits go to employees as AI memory demand lifts earnings. Micron reached a separate deal with its Taichung union the day before.

papers.title: Scaling Agentic Data for Long-Horizon Terminal Intelligence
papers.tldr: An automated pipeline builds long, realistic command-line tasks with the shortcuts removed, and a 27B open model trained on under 3,000 of them gains about 14 points on Terminal-Bench and keeps improving its work over 12-hour sessions.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors built an automatic factory for long, realistic command-line tasks, trained a mid-sized open model on about 2,900 worked examples, and got an agent that keeps working productively for hours.

## Background you need
A terminal agent is an AI that does work by typing commands into a computer's command line and reading the output. A trajectory is the full record of one session: every command, result and decision. Agents learn largely through supervised fine-tuning (training a model to imitate good trajectories).

## The problem
Real professional work at a terminal is long. An engineer gathers evidence, tries something, reads the error, changes plans and hands over a finished result. Most agent training data is short, so models rarely see that whole arc.

Making long tasks automatically is tricky. An AI building a practice environment often does the hard part by accident. In one example, the core function already exists, so "implement this feature" shrinks to changing one constant. Piling on requirements does not help, because new steps need not depend on earlier ones.

## The idea
Picture an exam writer who gives each new exam to a colleague who has never seen it. If the colleague finishes in five minutes, the writer checks why, finds the answer hidden in the question, and rewrites it. Only then does the writer add a follow-up part that builds on the first answers. TerminalHorizon runs this "outsider test, then patch the shortcut" loop on terminal tasks.

## How it works
1. **Find real work.** A planner agent picks behaviors still missing from the dataset. A research agent mines documentation, code and bug reports for real tasks. A builder agent packages each one with instructions, an environment, a reference solution and a hidden grader.
2. **Test with an outsider.** A separate "challenger" agent, not involved in building the task, tries to solve it from the public materials only. A review checks for crashes, leaked answers and unfair grading.
3. **Close the shortcuts.** The system compares the intended work with what the challenger actually did. If work was skipped, it traces the cause and rebuilds the environment so implementing and debugging are needed again.
4. **Grow the task in stages.** An evolution agent adds new requirements under the same goal. Each stage must depend on earlier results, for example by forcing the agent to inspect the current state.
5. **Record and train.** A strong teacher model, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, solves the tasks. The authors keep 2,852 trajectories from 1,535 environments across 25 domains, then fine-tune Qwen3.5-27B into TerminalHorizon-27B.

## Results
The trajectories average 52.8 back-and-forth turns, with 98 turns at the 90th percentile.

The trained model beats its base model on all 12 benchmarks tested. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, a standard test of command-line tasks, it scores 55.8%, up 14.2 points. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 it scores 60.67%, up 13.85 points. It also beats Terminal-Universe-27B, which used the same base model and about 32,000 trajectories, by 3 points. So it did better with less than a tenth of the data.

On AutomationBench, a business-automation test, the pass rate rises by 11.7 points. Math reasoning scores stay at or near their earlier levels. In 12-hour research case studies, the model kept experimenting after its first working answer and kept the improvements in its final output.

## Why it matters
Teams building coding and operations agents need data that teaches persistence and self-checking, not just quick fixes. This work suggests careful task design beats raw data volume. A 27-billion-parameter open model, small enough for many organizations to run, gets much better at long jobs.

## Caveats
All results come from one base model and one, much larger, teacher model. The pipeline uses many AI agents, so making the data is not cheap. Evidence for multi-hour autonomy rests on a few case studies, not a benchmark. The authors say gains had not leveled off, so the right amount of such data is still unknown.

## Key terms
- **Terminal agent**: an AI that completes tasks by running commands and reading the results.
- **Trajectory**: the step-by-step record of one agent session.
- **Long-horizon task**: a job needing many dependent steps over a long time.
- **Supervised fine-tuning**: extra training that teaches a model to copy good examples.
- **Terminal-Bench**: a public benchmark that scores agents on real command-line tasks.

papers.title: OasisKV: Scaling In-Decode KV Cache Beyond HBM with Lookahead Sparse Prefetching
papers.tldr: OasisKV stores a model's memory in CPU RAM and uses a draft model's next-token guess to prefetch only the needed pieces onto the GPU, roughly doubling serving throughput with under one point of accuracy loss.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
OasisKV keeps most of a language model's working memory in cheap computer memory and uses a fast "guess of the next word" to fetch only the pieces the GPU will need, just before it needs them.

## Background you need
When a language model writes, it saves notes about every earlier word in a KV cache (its short-term memory of what it has read). That cache lives in HBM, the small but very fast memory on the GPU. Decoding means producing the answer one token (a word piece) at a time. Speculative decoding uses a small helper model to guess upcoming tokens cheaply.

## The problem
The KV cache grows with every token. For a 32-billion-parameter model, one 32,700-token request needs about 8.6 GB. An 80 GB GPU then fits only about nine such requests at once, so long chats and long reasoning traces get expensive.

Moving the cache to ordinary CPU memory frees space, but fetching it back is slow. Pulling even 10% of the needed notes over the PCIe link (the cable between CPU and GPU) on demand noticeably slows each token.

## The idea
Think of a chef with a tiny counter and a big pantry. Fetching ingredients only when a recipe step calls for them stalls the cooking. A smart assistant reads one step ahead and fetches what will be needed next, while the chef keeps working.

OasisKV's assistant is the speculative-decoding helper. Its guess of the next token reveals which parts of memory the model will look at next.

## How it works
1. **Keep the full cache off the GPU.** All notes live in CPU memory. The GPU holds only a small working set: 128 blocks of 16 tokens, about 2,048 tokens, per attention head.
2. **Look one step ahead.** An existing draft model (EAGLE-3) proposes the next token. Its query runs through the same attention call as the real token, so no separate predictor is trained.
3. **Rank memory blocks.** Each block has a tiny summary, about one sixteenth of its size. The draft query scores every block, even ones not on the GPU, and picks the top ones. This guess matches the real next step's choice over 98% of the time.
4. **Fetch in the background.** Three helper workers predict, select and copy blocks on separate GPU streams. The main computation waits only for the layer it is about to run. A cap limits swaps per step so the link never jams.
5. **Extend across machines.** When one machine reads the prompt and another writes the answer, only the needed blocks are sent at first. Missing ones are fetched later, each at most once.

## Results
Accuracy stays close to full attention. On the LongBench v2 long-document test with Qwen3-8B, it scores 33.20 versus 33.60. On hard math and science reasoning, the average drops 0.35 points, while the older Quest and FreeKV methods lose 2.6 to 3.5 points.

On one H100 GPU, Qwen3-8B produces 2,083 tokens per second on AIME24 math problems, versus 1,235 for standard vLLM: 1.69 times the output on the same hardware. With 16,000-token contexts, it serves 90 to 95 requests at once instead of 22, for 2.1 times the throughput. For the large Qwen3-235B model on eight GPUs, the end-to-end gain is 1.20 times.

In the two-machine setup at 32,000 tokens, data sent per new request falls from 4.50 GB to 0.46 GB, about 9.7 times less.

## Why it matters
Long reasoning and long documents are where serving costs climb fastest. Fitting about four times as many users on one GPU cuts cost per answer. It reuses draft models many serving stacks already run.

## Caveats
The draft guesses are used only for prefetching and then thrown away, so the usual speed-up from speculative decoding is not yet added. Gains shrink on very large models and small batches. Fetching more than about 10% of blocks saturates the link. Some benefits, like faster first tokens, are estimated on paper, not measured. Competing systems ran on their own software stacks.

## Key terms
- **KV cache**: the model's stored notes about every earlier token.
- **HBM**: the GPU's small, very fast built-in memory.
- **Speculative decoding**: a cheap helper model guesses upcoming tokens for the big model to check.
- **Prefetching**: loading data before it is requested so nobody waits.
- **Throughput**: how many tokens the system produces per second across all users.

papers.title: A Self-Pruning Transformer: Extreme KV-Cache Compression with Universal Attention
papers.tldr: A new attention layer learns how fast each stored token should fade and deletes faded ones, cutting the model's memory by about 10–25× while matching or beating standard transformers.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors build a transformer layer that learns, during training, which past words it can safely forget, so its memory shrinks by roughly 10 to 25 times while answers stay as good or better.

## Background you need
A transformer reads text one token (a word piece) at a time. To avoid redoing work, it keeps a KV cache: the model's short-term memory of every token it has already read, stored in every layer. Attention is the step where each new token looks back over that memory to decide what matters. Pruning means throwing away cache entries the model will not need again.

## The problem
The KV cache grows with every token. For long documents it can become larger than the model itself. Common fixes are blunt. Eviction tools like H2O or SnapKV keep a fixed share of the cache, chosen in advance. "Forget gates" let old tokens fade, but they fade almost evenly, so the model ends up acting like it only sees a short sliding window of recent text.

## The idea
Think of a note-taker who marks each note with how quickly it should fade. Key names never fade; filler fades fast. Once a note is faded enough, it goes in the bin for good. Universal Attention (UA) teaches the model to set these fade rates itself. It then uses them as a signal for what to delete.

## How it works
1. **Add a learned fade score to attention.** Before attention picks which past tokens matter, UA adds a "decay" term that lowers the weight of older tokens.
2. **Combine three kinds of fading.** One gate depends on the current token (the reader). A new gate depends on each stored token, so every memory sets its own fade speed. A third term fades a token when newer tokens look very similar to it, since it has become redundant. The three are blended so that if any one says "keep this", the token is kept.
3. **Train everything together.** The gates and the rest of the model learn from ordinary next-word prediction.
4. **Delete at inference.** Each cached token carries a fade score that can only go down. When it drops below a threshold, the token is evicted permanently. That threshold is the only setting to tune, and each attention head decides on its own.

## Results
The team trained 1-billion-parameter models on 50 billion tokens and compared against standard Llama-style models, Mamba2, Gated DeltaNet and hybrids.
- On RULER, a long-context recall test at 4,000 tokens, UA scored 50.3 using a 21.4 MB cache. A standard Llama-style model scored 40.8 using 143.7 MB. So UA was more accurate with about one-seventh of the memory.
- Eviction tools keeping 10% of the cache scored only 7 to 28 on the same test.
- At 16,000 tokens, average compression on LongBench-E reached about 21× and up to 114× on some inputs. Scores moved by less than one point.
- On everyday reasoning tasks, accuracy matched or slightly beat the baseline, and text-prediction quality improved a little.

## Why it matters
Memory is often what caps how many users or how much text a GPU can handle. A model that decides on its own what to forget could serve longer documents on the same hardware.

## Caveats
- Models were trained from scratch at 1 billion parameters (3 billion in an appendix). Converting existing large models still shows a clear quality gap.
- UA is weaker on tasks that combine faint clues scattered across a whole document.
- Building the fade masks adds computing work.
- The memory savings are measured in bytes. Real speedups need a dedicated cache manager and sparse kernels, which are not yet built; the paper's own latency results are only preliminary.

## Key terms
- **KV cache:** stored keys and values for past tokens, reused so the model need not reread them.
- **Attention:** the step where a token weighs how relevant each earlier token is.
- **Decay gate:** a learned knob that makes older memories count less.
- **Pruning threshold:** the fade level below which a cached token is deleted.

papers.title: MpFA: Hardware-Efficient Train-Free QK4V8 FlashAttention Kernels on Blackwell GPUs
papers.tldr: A training-free attention kernel for NVIDIA Blackwell that mixes 4-bit and 8-bit math and keeps extra work off the slow softmax step, raising long-context output speed 2.81× over FlashAttention-4.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
MpFA is a faster attention routine for NVIDIA's new Blackwell GPUs that uses very low-precision numbers for part of the math, without retraining the model, and nearly triples output speed on long inputs.

## Background you need
Attention is the step in a language model where each token looks back over earlier tokens. FlashAttention is the standard fast code ("kernel", a small program that runs on the GPU) for this step; FA4 is its Blackwell version. Tensor cores are the GPU units that do matrix multiplication very fast. Precision is how many bits store each number: BF16 uses 16, FP8 uses 8 and NVFP4 uses 4. Fewer bits mean faster math but more rounding error.

## The problem
With long inputs, attention eats the GPU. On a B200 running Llama-3.1-8B at 128,000 tokens, attention took 72.5% of GPU time when reading the prompt and 91.4% when generating. Blackwell's 4-bit tensor cores promise about four times the throughput of 16-bit ones. Yet FA4 still uses 16-bit. Simply switching everything to 4-bit made attention slower, at 0.87× the speed of FA4. Retraining models for low precision is costly, and existing training-free methods target other chips.

## The idea
Speeding up only the multiplications is like widening the highway while leaving the toll booth alone. The authors found the toll booth: softmax, the step that turns raw scores into probabilities. It relies on exponentials that Blackwell did not speed up. In one test, the exponential alone took 417 cycles, more than both quantized multiplications together (384). So MpFA keeps every extra job off the softmax path.

## How it works
1. **Mix precisions.** Queries and keys (the vectors used to score relevance) use 4-bit. Probabilities and values use 8-bit. Running totals stay in 32-bit. In tests, this mix was 1.38× faster than FA4, while all 4-bit was slower.
2. **Use a fixed scale for probabilities.** Probabilities never exceed 1, so one constant scale works and no runtime measuring is needed. Tokens are read in reverse order so a very strong early token does not push other probabilities too close to zero.
3. **Fix errors on the tensor cores.** A few large outlier values hurt 4-bit accuracy. Earlier methods correct this by adding terms inside softmax, costing 18.6–22.7% of runtime. MpFA instead folds the correction into one small extra multiplication, which the fast tensor cores handle.
4. **Keep the hardware busy.** For prompt reading, it overlaps work in a fine-grained pipeline and reuses Blackwell's on-chip tensor memory. For generation, it splits the cache across more workers so the GPU stays full.

## Results
All tests ran on one NVIDIA B200 at 16,000 to 128,000 tokens.
- Prompt reading was 1.31–1.33× faster than FA4 and 1.15–1.17× faster than the 8-bit FlashInfer library.
- Token generation was 2.08× faster than FA4 on average.
- End-to-end output speed on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B rose 2.81× over FA4. A reply that took about 28 seconds would take about 10. The gain over 8-bit FlashInfer was smaller, 1.06×.
- Across ten model–task pairs from five benchmarks, the correction recovered 62.5% of the accuracy lost to low precision, for about 2% extra kernel time.
- The cache shrinks to about 1/2.56 of its 16-bit size.

## Why it matters
Long-context chat, code assistants and document tools spend most of their GPU time in attention. A drop-in, training-free kernel lets operators get more from Blackwell hardware without retraining.

## Caveats
- Tests covered one GPU type and two models of 8 to 14 billion parameters.
- Accuracy loss is reduced, not removed: about 37.5% of the drop remains.
- The edge over strong 8-bit kernels is modest end to end.
- The design relies on Blackwell-specific features, so it will not carry over directly to other chips.

## Key terms
- **Kernel:** a small program that runs a specific job on the GPU.
- **Softmax:** turns raw relevance scores into probabilities that sum to one.
- **Quantization:** storing numbers with fewer bits to save memory and time.
- **Prefill / decode:** reading the prompt versus generating new tokens one by one.
- **Outlier:** an unusually large value that wastes the range of a low-bit format.

papers.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
papers.tldr: A large study finds that a frozen general AI model can control robots well in simulation, but on real robots it is still too slow, costly and unreliable to count as practical embodied intelligence.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
A large research team took a frontier general-purpose AI model, GPT-6-Astra, and tested whether it can control real and simulated robots without any extra training, across 12 benchmarks and 8 physical robots.

## Background you need
Robots are usually driven by a VLA, a vision-language-action model (a network trained on robot recordings that turns camera images and an instruction into motor commands). Training one needs many teleoperated demonstrations, where a human remote-controls the robot. A general chat-style model has never been trained this way. It can still try to control a robot through a closed loop: look at camera frames, output a few actions, look again.

## The problem
Robotics benchmarks were designed for specialist robot models. Nobody knew how a frozen, general model would score on them, or what those scores would mean. A high benchmark number might hide huge costs or slow reactions. For a company deciding whether to build robots on top of general models, this gap matters a lot.

## The idea
The authors treat the general model like a new employee given a binder of notes before the shift. It studies the training demonstrations once, writes its own "knowledge package," and then works from that binder. A second, faster robot model acts like a skilled hand, while the general model acts like a careful supervisor. The authors borrow the "fast thinking versus slow thinking" framing: System 1 is fast reflexes, System 2 is slow reflection.

## How it works
1. **Self-written notes.** For each task, the model reads training demonstrations and writes a package with six parts. These include task guidance, motion and visual references, small helper programs, success checks and recovery steps. The package is then frozen, and the model's weights never change.
2. **More time.** The step limit is raised up to 10 times the official budget, inside the same episode. The robot can notice a miss and try again.
3. **Supervisor harness.** A fine-tuned VLA called π0.5 proposes hand movements. GPT-6-Astra reviews them before they run, either every step or every few steps.
4. **Real robots.** Eight platforms run zero-shot (no demonstrations). Humans write context such as joint limits and safety rules, and each trial gets about 60 minutes.
5. **A new test.** A simulated apartment where the clock keeps running while the model thinks.

## Results
The model matched or beat the best published scores on most settings. On DexJoCo (dexterous multi-finger hands) it reached 87.3%, roughly double the previous best. With extra time, it hit 81.9% on RoboDojo, a two-arm tabletop suite.

The harness study on RoboDojo is telling. The VLA alone scored 6.91%, and the general model alone scored 15.56%. Combining notes with supervised VLA control reached 54.17%, but used about 19.3 million tokens per episode. At the authors' rule of thumb of about 1 US dollar per million tokens, that is roughly 19 dollars per attempt.

Real robots were harder. Rigid pick-and-place worked 17 of 18 times. Cloth folding worked 2 of 4 times, and plug insertion failed all 11 tries. On the Unitree G1 humanoid, about 90% of each run was spent thinking. One nice surprise: a two-arm robot moved its free arm so its wrist camera could see into a vase before inserting a flower.

## Why it matters
This is a careful reality check for the "just use a big general model" approach to robotics. It shows general models now have real physical competence. It also shows where they still fail: speed, cost, and checking whether a task truly succeeded. Benchmark designers get a concrete proposal: no in-domain demonstrations, and a clock that keeps ticking.

## Caveats
Costs were not matched across compared systems. Some benchmarks had very few trials, so single runs can swing scores a lot. The notes packages transfer poorly to tasks unlike their source data. Real-robot results depend heavily on human-written context, which is effectively prompt engineering. In the apartment test, slow thinking let an egg burn and a fridge stay open. Hardware faults, like an overheating hand at 62 °C, ended trials the model could not recover from.

## Key terms
- **VLA (vision-language-action model):** a model that turns images and instructions into robot motor commands.
- **In-context learning:** improving on a task by reading examples in the prompt, without changing the model's weights.
- **Zero-shot:** doing a task with no task-specific examples.
- **Harness:** the surrounding software that connects a model to tools or robots and manages the loop.
- **Teleoperation:** a human remote-controlling a robot to record demonstrations.
- **Token:** a small chunk of text or data; model usage is billed per token.

papers.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
papers.tldr: An open, training-free toolkit gives image-reading AI models perception tools, web search, code and a shared evidence memory, raising scores by about 10 to 13 points across 22 benchmarks at lower cost than thinking longer.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
OpenVLHarness is a ready-made toolkit that lets an image-understanding AI model zoom, measure, search the web and run code, while keeping every piece of evidence in a shared memory it can reuse.

## Background you need
A multimodal large language model, or MLLM, is a chatbot-style model that can read images as well as text. Many hard visual questions need more than looking, such as counting 40 objects or checking a fact online. A "harness" is the software around a model that hands it tools and runs the loop of asking, acting and reading results. "Tool use" means the model writes a request, a separate program does the work, and the result comes back.

## The problem
The authors first tried the obvious fix: let the model think longer. On 22 benchmarks, a bigger reasoning budget gave only modest gains. Thinking harder cannot replace a missing measurement or an outside fact.

Existing tool setups have their own issues. Tool outputs come in messy formats, like masks, depth maps or raw web pages. If the model cannot read them easily, or forgets them a step later, the tools barely help. Teams building visual assistants often end up writing this glue code by hand for every project.

## The idea
Think of a detective with a well-organized evidence locker. Each lab report, photo and witness note gets a label and a shelf. The detective does not re-run the lab test each time. They pull the labeled item and compare it with others. OpenVLHarness gives the model that locker, plus a common way to request work from every lab.

## How it works
1. **One front desk for many tools.** A "capability layer" offers nine task-level tools. These include object grounding (finding and outlining objects, using Segment Anything), text reading in images, depth estimation, camera position across photos, zoom-in, text search, reverse image search and webpage visits.
2. **Readable results.** Each tool's raw output is turned into something the model can digest, like an annotated image, a short summary or a compact table of numbers.
3. **Persistent memory.** Images, boxes, masks, depth maps and web links are stored as labeled items for the whole question. The model can refer to them by name in later steps.
4. **Code over evidence.** A coding helper writes and runs Python on the stored items. For example, it can count boxes or compare depths precisely, instead of guessing in its head.
5. **No retraining.** The underlying model stays unchanged. Any model that supports tool calls can be plugged in.

## Results
Tests covered 22 benchmarks in four groups: counting and grounding, web search and deep research, general visual question answering with hallucination checks, and spatial understanding. Across eight backbone models, open and proprietary, average scores rose 9.7 to 12.6 points over the same model without tools.

Some examples, as averages out of 100: Qwen3-VL-8B went from 34.2 to 45.4. Qwen3-VL-32B went from 38.3 to 50.9. GPT-6 Astra, the strongest base model, went from 60.3 to 70.2.

Cost results are notable. GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, inside the harness, scored 56.5. That beat the plain model, the Codex coding agent and the Visual Sketchpad tool system at maximum effort. It did so using at most 37% of their model-token cost. In plain terms, a better answer for roughly a third of the bill.

On the small Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the untrained harness scored 33.5. Three systems specially trained for tool use scored between 25.0 and 28.0.

## Why it matters
Builders of visual assistants get an open, reusable base instead of custom glue code. The results suggest better tools and memory can be cheaper than buying more thinking time. Researchers also get a shared setup to compare models fairly on tool-heavy tasks.

## Caveats
Performance depends on outside services, such as a search API and several perception models, which may fail or change. Results for the large proprietary models come from single runs, so their run-to-run variation is unknown. Memory resets for each question, so the system does not learn across tasks. Handling conflicts between evidence sources and tool reliability remain open problems.

## Key terms
- **MLLM (multimodal large language model):** a language model that also understands images.
- **Harness:** the software loop that connects a model to tools and manages their results.
- **Grounding:** finding where an object named in text appears in an image.
- **Depth estimation:** guessing how far each pixel is from the camera.
- **Backbone:** the core model plugged into the harness.
- **Token cost:** the price of a model's input and output text, billed per small chunk.
